lesson_title: Weigh the Whole Train First: Connected Bodies and Pulleys
hook_text: The rope holding a falling bucket pulls with LESS than the bucket's weight. Here's why that's the whole question.
clip_script: Two shopping trolleys tied together. You push the front one, the back one follows — and every connected-bodies question in the paper is hiding in that picture. Three facts. They share ONE acceleration, because the rope can't stretch. The rope pulls equally at both ends, because it's light. And a rope can only pull, never push. Now the clever bit. That rope tugs the back trolley forward and drags the front trolley back, same size, opposite ways. So if you treat the two trolleys as ONE object, the rope cancels completely. It vanishes. That gives you the recipe. Move one: add the masses, add only the outside forces, forget the rope, divide — there's your acceleration. Move two: go back to ONE object, the lazy one with fewest forces, and the rope tension pops out in a single line. And the answer everyone gets wrong: a 6 kilogram mass falling on a string weighs 58 comma 8 newtons, but the string only pulls with 29 comma 4. It has to pull less — otherwise nothing would fall.
visual_style: Two supermarket trolleys roped together rolling down an aisle, with the rope arrows lighting up and then annihilating each other; cut to a bucket falling on a rope over a pulley with the two numbers compared side by side.
mood: Practical and slightly triumphant — a hard question type revealed to be two easy lines.
pacing: Quick setup, deliberate pause on the cancelling arrows, fast recipe, surprise ending.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and solve any two-body pulley question in two moves.
